newsitem.title: SPAIN: FORECAST - Spain's CPI to set new record on February.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Spain's CPI to set new record on February.

text.p: Spain's February consumer price inflation index (CPI) is expected to fall to post another record low, but analysts remained divided about whether the Bank of Spain would reward the achievement with a cut in its key money market rate.
A Reuter poll of analysts forecasts February inflation, due on Thursday, to inch up 0.2 percent to a 2.8-percent yearly rate, which would be below January's 28-year low of 2.9 percent.
Though analysts still see the downtrend intact for at least a few more months, they said a possible turnaround in the second half and peseta weakness should make the central bank cautious.
"The CPI cycle seems to be close to bottoming out...The recent dollar and raw materials increase will have soon an effect," said Gregorio Gomez at All Trading here.

"Look at the market's reaction after recent CPI announcements. In the last few months, (debt) prices only move a bit. Before, it was not like that. Bonos have already priced in all good news over inflation," he added.
Lower phone tariffs, olive oil and seasonal falls in fresh food are seen as the main factors keeping inflation cool this month, analysts said.

"We expect core inflation to increase 0.23 percent, with energy prices up 0.2 percent and food down 1.22 percent, as is normal in this season," said Toni Espasa, economist at University Carlos III in Madrid.

Espasa, who expects February CPI to rise about 0.06 percent to a 2.70-percent year-on-year rate with core inflation at 2.5 percent, said February data would not add any fresh information as the overall picture remains the same.
"We still see Spain's CPI declining to close to two percent in May then, it could be back to 2.6 percent for the end of December to rise to 3.0 percent in 1998," he said.

Despite stark improvement, CPI still did not meet economic requirements for joining the single currency. So, it was unlikely that even a good number would prompt the central bank to ease, San Paolo bank in London said in a note to clients.
"This slightly concerning news on CPI, coupled with the the recent weakness in the peseta is likely to encourage the Bank of Spain to keep rates on hold in the near term," it wrote.
But not all analysts share such a bearish view.

"We are more optimistic...this could back a cut in the key money market rate," said Alfredo Urrutia, chief economist at Societe Generale who sees February prices up 0.1 percent for a yearly rate of 2.6 percent. "If inflation falls...it is possible that the Bank of Spain would then cut rates by 25 basis points."
The Bank of Spain will announce its repurchase agreement result on Friday.
Although many analysts saw peseta weakness preventing a Bank of Spain rate cut, Urrutia said a possible easing would bring new confidence to the Spanish unit.
"It would be like saying to the market that convergence or not..EMU on time or not, what is important is that Spain's macroeconomy is doing fine, and that matters," Urrutia said.
At 0845 GMT, the peseta was at 84.76/77 per mark versus 84.82/84 at Monday's close.

The Bank of Spain has built up its currency reserves while cutting its key interest rate to six percent from nine percent at the start of 1996. January reserves rose to a maximum $65.29 billion from 39.44 billion a year ago.
But in February, central bank currency reserves fell $483.6 million to $3.46 billion due to Bank of Spain efforts to buy pesetas and to defend its unit.
